content: A developing country is characterized by a relatively low standard of living, an underdeveloped industrial base, and moderate to low scores on the Human Development Index (HDI) and per capita income. These nations are in a phase of economic development. However, not all countries classified as developing fit this description, as some developing nations are more advanced than certain developed countries. Nations with economies that are more advanced than other developing countries but not yet fully developed are referred to as newly industrialized countries (NICs). Additionally, developing countries that have shown consistent economic growth and exhibit strong economic potential are termed emerging markets. Examples of Big Emerging Market (BEM) economies include Argentina, Brazil, China, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Poland, Russia, South Africa, South Korea, and Turkey. The term developing country is not always appropriate for all nations that are not classified as developed. Some poorer countries have experienced prolonged economic decline and are instead categorized as least developed countries (LDCs) or failed states. Development is typically associated with the presence of modern infrastructure, both physical and institutional, and a shift away from low-value-added sectors such as agriculture and natural resource extraction. In contrast, developed countries generally have economic systems based on continuous, self-sustaining growth in the tertiary and quaternary sectors, along with high standards of living. Developing countries are generally those that have not achieved significant industrialization relative to their population size and have a low standard of living. There is a strong correlation between low income levels and high population growth rates. Various terms are used to describe developing countries, including less developed countries (LDCs), least economically developed countries (LEDCs), underdeveloped nations, Third World nations, and non-industrialized nations. Conversely, developed countries are referred to as most economically developed countries (MEDCs), First World nations, or industrialized nations. To address the euphemistic nature of the term developing, international organizations have adopted the term less economically developed countries (LEDCs) to describe the poorest nations, which cannot be considered developing in any meaningful sense. LEDCs represent the poorest subset of LDCs. This distinction also helps to counter the misconception that the standard of living is uniform across the developing world. The concept of a developing nation is present in various theoretical frameworks, including decolonization theories, liberation theology, Marxism, anti-imperialism, and political economy. Critics argue that the term developing can be misleading. In the context of countries that were historically affected by European colonialism, the term re-developing may be more accurate, as many of these nations had successful economic systems prior to colonization. However, Western analysts often dismiss these pre-colonial systems as invalid or not developed, reflecting an ethnocentric bias that equates development with Western-style progress. Emerging and developing economies, as identified by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in its World Economic Outlook Report, include a wide range of nations. These countries are often grouped into categories based on their level of development. For example, newly industrialized countries (NICs) are those with economies that are more advanced than other developing nations but not yet fully developed. Examples of NICs include Brazil, China, India, Malaysia, Mexico, the Philippines, South Africa, Thailand, and Turkey. Big Emerging Market (BEM) economies include Argentina, Brazil, China, Egypt, India, Indonesia, Jordan, Mexico, Poland, Russia, South Africa, South Korea, and Turkey. Some countries have inconsistent records of development, such as many nations in Africa, Central America, and the Caribbean (with exceptions like Jamaica and Puerto Rico). Other countries, such as Laos and Cambodia in Southeast Asia, also fall into this category. Approximately 76% of the world's nations are classified as having inconsistent development. Additionally, there are countries experiencing long-term civil wars, large-scale breakdowns in the rule of law, or governance by non-development-oriented dictatorships. These nations, often referred to as failed states, include Afghanistan, Haiti, Somalia, Myanmar, Iraq, and North Korea. Many of these countries also suffer from low resource availability.
